title: The Septuagint and Jewish-Hellenistic Identity
content:
The Septuagint and Jewish-Hellenistic Identity
The Letter of Aristeas is a fascinating pseudepigraphic work that grants religious and cultural legitimacy to the Septuagint, presenting it as equal in value to the Hebrew original. The work serves as a founding myth for Alexandrian Jewry, combining an ostensibly historical story about the initiative of King Ptolemy II with Jewish apologetics that presents the Torah as the pinnacle of wisdom and rationality. Through utopian descriptions of Jerusalem and philosophical dialogues between Jewish sages and the Hellenistic ruler, the author builds an ideological bridge that allows Jews to integrate into the Greek world without abandoning their unique identity. Ultimately, the letter establishes the conception that Judaism is an exalted philosophical and moral religion, which enriches universal culture and wins the esteem of the enlightened of the ancient world.
The Essence, Structure and Influence of the Letter of Aristeas: A Comprehensive Study of the Founding Myth of the Septuagint and of Jewish-Hellenistic Identity
The Letter of Aristeas, known in scholarship also as the work "Aristeas to Philocrates," is one of the most complex and influential documents in the Jewish literature of the Second Temple period. The work, shaped as a pseudepigraphic letter, is not merely a historical report on the beginnings of the Septuagint, but a multilayered literary creation that seeks to bridge the cultural and religious gap between the world of the Bible and the Hellenistic culture surrounding Alexandrian Jewry.[1, 2, 3] Through the story of Aristeas, ostensibly a Hellenistic official at the court of King Ptolemy II Philadelphus, an entire world of apologetics, political philosophy, and utopian descriptions of Jerusalem and the Temple is revealed to the reader.[3, 4, 5]
Modern scholarship sees the Letter of Aristeas as a "founding myth" (charter myth) of Jewish-Alexandrian society. It was intended to grant religious and cultural legitimacy to the translation of the Torah into Greek, placing it as equal in value to the Hebrew original.[3, 6, 7] Beyond that, it serves as a tool for presenting Judaism as a rational, moral and exalted religion, capable not only of surviving within the Hellenistic world but even of enriching it with its wisdom.[7, 8] The present report will examine in depth the structure of the work, the question of its authenticity, the historical and archaeological contexts that emerge from it, and its decisive influence on the perception of the Bible throughout the generations.
The Literary Architecture and the Question of Genre
The Letter of Aristeas is not a "letter" in the narrow sense of the word. Although it opens with an address to Philocrates and closes with a promise of further correspondence, it lacks the formal features of the epistolary genre, such as opening formulas of greeting or reference to the physical distance between the addressee and the writer.[3] Instead, it is a work that combines many literary genres: historiography, travel descriptions (ekphrasis), philosophical dialogues reminiscent of the Greek symposium, and Jewish wisdom literature.[3]
The structure of the work is carefully planned to lead the reader from the universal context of the great library of Alexandria into the sanctuary in Jerusalem, and back to Alexandria as a center of shared Jewish-Hellenistic wisdom.[4, 7] The work can be divided into four central axes, each of which serves a distinct ideological purpose:
The combination of these components creates a work that does not merely tell a story, but builds a logical and emotional argument in favor of Jewish existence in the Greek world. The author uses techniques of Hellenistic historians, including the incorporation of ostensibly official documents (letters from the king to the high priest and the replies of Eleazar), in order to give the story credibility and royal splendor.[3, 13]
The Question of Authorship and Dating: The Shift from Documentation to Pseudepigraphy
For more than 1,500 years the Letter of Aristeas was regarded as a reliable firsthand historical source. Central figures such as Philo of Alexandria, Josephus (Yosef ben Matityahu) and the Church Fathers relied on it to explain the origin of the Septuagint.[6, 14, 15] However, with the rise of historical criticism in the Renaissance, scholars such as Juan Luis Vives and Humphrey Hody began to expose glaring contradictions in the text.[3]
Today there is a broad scholarly consensus that the author is not the Greek Aristeas, but an educated Alexandrian Jew, who apparently lived in the second half of the second century BCE.[1, 3, 6] Several factors led to this conclusion:
First, the chronological failure concerning Demetrius of Phalerum. The work presents Demetrius as the chief librarian and close adviser of Ptolemy II Philadelphus. However, external historical sources (such as Cicero and Diogenes Laertius) attest that Demetrius, who was identified with the reign of Ptolemy I, was exiled from Egypt immediately upon the accession of Ptolemy II to the throne and died shortly thereafter.[3, 11, 15, 16] Such an error is not plausible for a court official who lived at that time, but it makes sense for a later author who seeks to link two famous figures of the Alexandrian golden age.[3, 17]
Second, the linguistic analysis of the text. The Greek of the letter includes administrative terms and court titles (such as "chief of the bodyguards" in the plural) that do not appear in papyri and inscriptions before the middle of the second century BCE.[3, 18] Likewise, the author's deep familiarity with the details of Jewish halakha, the reasons for the commandments and the structure of the Temple betrays his identity as a Jew seeking to present his religion in a positive light, and not as an idol-worshipping Greek observing from the side.[6, 8, 14, 17]
The Royal Negotiation and the Release of the Captives: An Act of Cosmic Justice
The narrative of the letter opens with a cultural initiative of wide scope. Demetrius of Phalerum presents to King Ptolemy II the need to translate the laws of the Jews in order to complete the project of the "universal library."[4, 7] Demetrius notes that the library numbers more than 200,000 volumes and aspires to reach 500,000.[7, 13, 19] This description gives the Jewish Torah the status of a world cultural asset, without which the royal collection is considered incomplete.[7]
Within this royal context, the author weaves in a dramatic event: the release of more than 100,000 Jews who had been held captive in Egypt.[4, 5, 6, 19] Aristeas, addressing the king in the name of justice, argues that the Jews cannot be asked to translate their laws while their fellow people languish in slavery under the same rule.[3, 19] The king not only grants the request, but allocates enormous sums from the state treasury to compensate the slave owners.[4, 13, 19]
This act is analyzed by scholars as a "New Exodus Story."[20] Unlike the biblical Pharaoh who hardened his heart, Ptolemy II is presented as the model of the enlightened Hellenistic ruler who recognizes the supremacy of the Jewish God.[20, 21] The release of the slaves serves as proof that it is possible to live under foreign rule in prosperity and freedom, as long as the ruler respects the Jewish religion.[20, 22] This is a central message for the Jews of Alexandria: loyalty to the kingdom does not contradict loyalty to the Torah, since the king himself sees the Torah as a source of truth and justice.[7, 22]
Jerusalem and the Temple: A Display of Splendor and Rationality
A large part of the letter is devoted to a description of the delegation's journey to Jerusalem.[4, 9] This description, called in scholarship ekphrasis, was intended to illustrate to the Alexandrian reader the beauty and importance of the religious center in Judea.[3, 8] The author describes Jerusalem as a wisely planned city, situated on a high mountain and well fortified.[10, 11]
The Temple is presented as a focus of technological efficiency and aesthetic splendor:
The sophisticated water system: the author marvels at a natural spring gushing from within the Temple (a description that does not match the geological reality of the Temple Mount, but serves the idealization) and at a system of underground cisterns connected by lead pipes.[10, 18, 23] This system makes possible the immediate washing away of the blood of the sacrifices, so that the Temple always remains clean and dignified.[4, 10]
Quiet and order in the service: the description of the priests' service stresses the self-discipline and silence in which the rites are performed. Despite the thousands of participants, not a sound is heard, which attests to the awe and holiness of the place.[9, 10]
The citadel (the Akra): the description of the military citadel overlooking the Temple was intended to reassure the reader that the sanctuary is well protected against external attacks or internal revolts.[4, 9, 10]
Scholars point out that these descriptions are influenced by the Greek travel literature of the period.[3, 18] The author tries to prove that the Temple in Jerusalem is not a site of barbaric or strange worship, but an institution run according to the highest standards of Hellenistic culture: in beauty, in order and in engineering wisdom.[8, 21]
Eleazar's Speech: The Torah as a Moral Protective Wall
One of the intellectual high points of the letter is the conversation between Aristeas and Eleazar the high priest concerning the nature of the Torah.[4, 9] Aristeas asks a question that represents Hellenistic puzzlement: why does the Torah include laws that seem petty or strange, such as certain dietary prohibitions, when all the animals were created by the same God?[9]
Eleazar's answer is a masterpiece of allegorical apologetics. He explains that the lawgiver (Moses) did not establish these laws because of physical qualities of the animals, but as an educational and moral means.[9] The laws of kashrut and separation were intended to create an "iron wall" that would prevent the Jews from mingling with idol-worshipping peoples whose morals are corrupt.[4, 6, 9]
Eleazar interprets the prohibitions symbolically:
The forbidden birds of prey represent tyranny and violence, and abstaining from eating them teaches the Jew to pursue peace and justice.[4, 9]
The animals that chew the cud and have split hooves represent the need for constant remembrance of God and for distinguishing between good and evil.[9]
This move turns the practical commandments from a ritual burden into a profound philosophical system. The author argues that Judaism is the most rational religion, since every detail in it is intended to lead to moral perfection and a life of justice.[7, 8] This conception enabled the Alexandrian Jews to continue observing the commandments while feeling themselves full partners in the world of Greek thought.[7, 22]
The Symposium in Alexandria: The Superiority of Jewish Wisdom
After the arrival of the 72 elders (six from each tribe) in Egypt, King Ptolemy holds in their honor a series of banquets lasting seven days.[3, 4, 5, 6] Each evening the king addresses questions to ten of the elders, dealing with broad topics of leadership, ethics and statecraft.[4, 5, 21]

The elders' answers leave the king and the court philosophers astounded by their wisdom.[4, 7, 21] The message that emerges from the symposium is unequivocal: Jewish wisdom is not limited to the study hall or the Temple; it is relevant to, and even superior to, every Hellenistic doctrine of the state.[7] The elders are presented as the perfect philosopher-statesmen, combining a broad Greek education with firm moral foundations that originate in the Torah.[3, 7, 17]
The symposium also serves to define the figure of the ideal king. According to Aristeas, the good king is one who subordinates his will to the divine moral laws and sees his subjects as human beings equal before God.[5, 7] This is a veiled criticism of Hellenistic tyranny, formulated as friendly advice to a king who respects Judaism.[5, 6]
The Act of Translation: From the Hebrew to the Greek Scripture
The last and most famous part of the letter describes the process of the translation itself. The elders are led to the island of Pharos, a place cut off from the bustle of the city, where they devote themselves to the sacred task.[3, 4] They work in the morning hours, pray and wash their hands in the sea as a sign of purity, and afterwards gather to compare their versions of the translation.[3, 4, 19]
The author stresses that the translation was the result of collective agreement (consensus).[3, 7] Demetrius of Phalerum supervises the writing, and every sentence set down in writing is approved by all 72 elders.[7] The work was completed after exactly 72 days, a perfect correspondence between the number of those who performed it and its duration, which hints at divine providence without any need for descriptions of open miracles.[2, 6, 7]
Upon the completion of the work, an event of decisive importance takes place: the reading of the translation before the Jewish community of Alexandria.[4, 6, 12] The assembly, which includes the city's notables and the whole people, declares the translation "good and beautiful" and pronounces a curse (anathema) on anyone who tries to add to it, subtract from it or change anything in it.[4, 6, 7, 12]
This step grants the Septuagint the status of a "holy book" standing in its own right.[7] For the Jews of Alexandria, the Greek Torah is not merely a "translation" in the modern sense, but a renewed revelation of the word of God in a language they understand.[2, 25] The curse was intended to preserve this text as the canonical and sole text, similar to the warnings that appear in the book of Deuteronomy concerning the original Torah.[7]
The Historical and Social Context: A Founding Myth for a Changing Society
To understand the Letter of Aristeas in depth, one must examine the social reality of the Jews of Egypt in the second century BCE.[1, 3, 22] The Jewish community of Alexandria was one of the wealthiest and most educated in the ancient world, but it faced a twofold challenge:
On the one hand, the need to defend itself against cultural and religious attacks by Egyptian and Hellenistic writers (such as Manetho), who presented the Jews as descendants of lepers expelled from Egypt.[6] The Letter of Aristeas answers these attacks by presenting Judaism as a religion that won the admiration of the greatest kings and by emphasizing the importance of Jerusalem as a world center.[6, 22]
On the other hand, the need to prevent total assimilation into the attractive Greek culture.[1, 8] The author addresses educated young Jews ("Philocrates, lover of learning") and tries to persuade them that they need not abandon their heritage in order to be successful philosophers or courtiers.[7, 8] The Torah, he argues, is the very source of all the wisdom in which the Greeks pride themselves.[7]
The letter thus serves as a two-way bridge: it "sells" Judaism to the Greek world, and gives the Jews an intellectual basis for their continued existence as a proud minority within the empire.[3, 7, 22]
The Letter of Aristeas Tested by Archaeology and Geography
Although the letter is a literary work with ideological aims, it contains details that allow it to be cross-checked against the archaeological reality of the Land of Israel and of Alexandria.[3, 18]
The water system in Jerusalem: the detailed description of the cisterns and lead pipes in the Temple has received much attention from scholars.[10, 18, 26] Archaeological finds confirm that in the Second Temple period aqueducts were built that carried water from Solomon's Pools (near Bethlehem) to the Temple Mount.[26, 27, 28] Although the claim of a natural spring within the Temple precinct is geologically incorrect, it reflects the admiration for the abundance of water that was available at the site for the needs of worship and purity.[23, 26]
The Akra (the citadel): the description of the citadel that guarded the Temple fits a reality in which citadels stood north of the Temple Mount (such as the Birah fortress or, later, the Antonia).[10, 11, 29] The author stresses that the citadel was in the hands of loyal Jews, which may hint at a period in which the Jews had broad religious and security autonomy.[11]
Agriculture and demography: the letter describes Judea as a fertile and densely populated land, and mentions the policy of encouraging Jews to remain in the rural areas rather than migrate to the large cities (so as not to harm agricultural production).[18] These details match the economic reality of the Ptolemaic and early Hasmonean period.[18]
The library of Alexandria: the letter is the earliest source that explicitly mentions the great library of Alexandria.[6] Despite the chronological inaccuracies concerning Demetrius, the description of the Ptolemaic kings' aspiration to gather all the wisdom of the world in one library is regarded as a faithful reflection of the cultural ideology of that period.[7, 19]
Influence and Reception: From Josephus to Modern Criticism
The influence of the Letter of Aristeas on Jewish and Christian historiography and theology was immense.
In the Jewish world: Josephus quoted extensive parts of the letter in his book "Antiquities of the Jews," thereby establishing the story as part of the official history of the people of Israel.[4, 5, 6] Philo of Alexandria gave the story a more prophetic coloring, claiming that the translators were prophets who produced an identical text by miracle.[3, 15] Echoes of the story also appear in rabbinic literature (as in Tractate Megillah), but there the attitude toward the day of the translation is more complex: at times it is presented as an achievement vis-à-vis the kingdom and at times as a hard day for Israel.[3, 30]
In the Christian world: the Church Fathers saw in the letter proof that the Septuagint is the authorized and exclusive translation of the Bible.[3, 12, 14] For them, the fact that a gentile king initiated the translation and that Eleazar the high priest approved it gave legitimacy to the Church's use of the Greek Bible instead of the Hebrew original.[12, 14]
In modern scholarship: in the 20th and 21st centuries the focus of research shifted from an attempt to extract "historical facts" about the translation to the analysis of the letter as an ideological work.[3, 17, 31] Scholars such as Benjamin Wright and Moses Hadas provided in-depth interpretations showing how the letter reflects the tensions and hopes of Diaspora Jewry.[17, 31, 32]
Conclusions and Summary Insights
The Letter of Aristeas is much more than a story about the translation of a book; it is evidence of the boldest and most impressive attempt of the ancient world to create a synthesis between two giant cultures.[1, 7, 22] Through the figure of Aristeas, the author succeeded in creating a space in which the Jewish Torah becomes universal wisdom, Jerusalem becomes a utopia of order and cleanliness, and Alexandria becomes a center in which the king and the Jewish sage cooperate for the sake of truth.[4, 7, 8]
The central insights that emerge from the comprehensive study of the letter are:
The Torah as a world cultural asset: the letter established the conception that Jewish law is not merely an internal matter of a small people, but a document of importance for all humanity, worthy of a place of honor in the greatest library in the world.[7]
Legitimacy for the Diaspora: the work provides a religious and cultural justification for life in the Diaspora, while maintaining a deep bond with the center in the Land of Israel. It proves that one can speak Greek and think like a Greek, and still remain entirely faithful to the covenant of Sinai.[3, 22]
Allegory as a bridging tool: the use of allegorical interpretation of the commandments (as presented in Eleazar's speech) paved the way for later Jewish thought, including Philo of Alexandria and the Jewish philosophy of the Middle Ages.[3, 9]
Constructing textual authority: the curse pronounced on changing the translation shows an early awareness of the importance of a fixed and authoritative text, a step that was vital for the survival of the Jewish religion in the passage between languages and cultures.[7, 25]
All in all, the Letter of Aristeas remains a foundational document that teaches us not only about the origin of the Septuagint, but about the power of literature to create identity, to bridge gaps and to make an ancient tradition always relevant, even in the very heart of a foreign culture.[3, 5, 12]
